ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Sixteen university students were assigned by block randomization to watch either a 40-minute action-film clip (n = 8) or a 40-minute nature documentary (n = 8).
Participants were eligible if they were university students, understood English (the questionnaire and stimuli were in English), and gave informed consent.
At post-test, participants were asked to respond according to how they were thinking and feeling at that moment.
Participants gave written informed consent and received a general description of the study without the specific hypotheses, to limit demand characteristics.
Participants were then debriefed, the reason for withholding the hypotheses was explained, and they were reminded that participation was voluntary and that they could withdraw their data.
Sixteen participants completed the REI-40 before and after viewing (documentary group n = 8; action-film group n = 8), and there were no missing participants.
All participants gave written informed consent before taking part, were told that participation was voluntary, and were debriefed afterwards.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Sixteen university students were assigned by block randomization to watch either a 40-minute action-film clip (n = 8) or a 40-minute nature documentary (n = 8).

> Participants were eligible if they were university students, understood English (the questionnaire and stimuli were in English), and gave informed consent.

> At post-test, participants were asked to respond according to how they were thinking and feeling at that moment.

> Participants gave written informed consent and received a general description of the study without the specific hypotheses, to limit demand characteristics.

> Participants were then debriefed, the reason for withholding the hypotheses was explained, and they were reminded that participation was voluntary and that they could withdraw their data.

> Sixteen participants completed the REI-40 before and after viewing (documentary group n = 8; action-film group n = 8), and there were no missing participants.

> All participants gave written informed consent before taking part, were told that participation was voluntary, and were debriefed afterwards.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Whether brief media exposure can shift how people describe their own thinking is poorly understood.
This pilot experiment tested whether watching an action-film clip changed self-reported rational and experiential thinking styles relative to an active comparison condition.
Sixteen university students were assigned by block randomization to watch either a 40-minute action-film clip (n = 8) or a 40-minute nature documentary (n = 8).
All completed the Rational-Experiential Inventory-40 (REI-40) immediately before and after viewing.
A 2 (Group) × 2 (Time) mixed ANOVA showed no Group × Time interaction for rational ability, rational engagement, or experiential engagement (all p ≥ .270).
An interaction emerged for experiential ability, F(1, 14) = 4.94, p = .043, η²p = .26, but it did not survive correction for four outcomes (Holm-adjusted p = .173).
It also reflected a decline in the documentary group (-2.88 points) and no change in the action-film group (-0.12), and the subscale had poor internal consistency.
The groups did not differ at post-test on any subscale, and results were unchanged after adjusting for pre-test scores.
The study found no evidence that an action-film clip changed self-reported thinking styles relative to a nature documentary.
With eight participants per group, only very large effects could have been detected, so the results are inconclusive about small and moderate effects.
Larger, bettermatched studies with manipulation checks and behavioral measures of reasoning are needed.
Films, series, and short videos are a routine part of everyday life, and audiences follow fictional characters through danger, conflict, and difficult choices.
Several lines of media research suggest that such exposure can leave short-term traces.
Identification refers to temporarily adopting a character's perspective, emotions, and goals (Cohen, 2001).
text.formatted: Identification refers to temporarily adopting a character's perspective, emotions, and goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Cohen, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Narrative transportation refers to becoming mentally and emotionally absorbed in a story and is linked to acceptance of story-consistent beliefs (Green & Brock, 2000); a meta-analysis of 132 effect sizes from 76 articles has mapped its antecedents and consequences (van Laer et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Narrative transportation refers to becoming mentally and emotionally absorbed in a story and is linked to acceptance of story-consistent beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Green & Brock, 2000)</ref>; a meta-analysis of 132 effect sizes from 76 articles has mapped its antecedents and consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(van Laer et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Tal-Or and Cohen (2010) treated identification and transportation as distinct processes and manipulated each.
text.formatted: Tal-Or and <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Cohen (2010)</ref> treated identification and transportation as distinct processes and manipulated each.

text.text: Media priming research examines the short-term influence of media exposure on later judgments and behavior (Roskos-Ewoldsen et al., 2007), and social cognitive theory adds that people learn from models presented in mass media (Bandura, 2001).
text.formatted: Media priming research examines the short-term influence of media exposure on later judgments and behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Roskos-Ewoldsen et al., 2007)</ref>, and social cognitive theory adds that people learn from models presented in mass media <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bandura, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: What remains unclear is whether a short period of narrative viewing can shift something as basic as the way people describe their own thinking.
Cognitive-experiential self-theory (CEST) offers a framework for this question.

CEST proposes two interacting information-processing systems: a rational system that is deliberate, analytic, verbal, and effortful, and an experiential system that is intuitive, automatic, associative, and emotion-linked (Epstein, 1994).
text.formatted: CEST proposes two interacting information-processing systems: a rational system that is deliberate, analytic, verbal, and effortful, and an experiential system that is intuitive, automatic, associative, and emotion-linked <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Epstein, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: The systems are treated as distinct rather than as opposite ends of one dimension, so a person can enjoy analytic thinking and also trust intuition.
Related dual-process accounts distinguish fast, automatic processing from slow, reflective processing (Evans, 2008; Kahneman, 2011), although these accounts are not identical to CEST.
text.formatted: Related dual-process accounts distinguish fast, automatic processing from slow, reflective processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Evans, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Kahneman, 2011)</ref>, although these accounts are not identical to CEST.

text.text: The Rational-Experiential Inventory (REI) was developed to measure individual differences in the two systems (Epstein et al., 1996).
text.formatted: The Rational-Experiential Inventory (REI) was developed to measure individual differences in the two systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Epstein et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Its original scales, Need for Cognition and Faith in Intuition, formed two orthogonal factors. Pacini and Epstein (1999) introduced a revised version with separate ability and engagement subscales: rational ability (perceived capacity to reason logically), rational engagement (enjoyment of effortful thinking), experiential ability (confidence in intuitive judgment), and experiential engagement (reliance on and enjoyment of intuition).
text.formatted: Its original scales, Need for Cognition and Faith in Intuition, formed two orthogonal factors. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Pacini and Epstein (1999)</ref> introduced a revised version with separate ability and engagement subscales: rational ability (perceived capacity to reason logically), rational engagement (enjoyment of effortful thinking), experiential ability (confidence in intuitive judgment), and experiential engagement (reliance on and enjoyment of intuition).

text.text: The REI measures self-perceived abilities and preferences, not reasoning performance.

Whether these self-perceptions can vary with immediate context is an open empirical question. Pacini and Epstein (1999) noted that both situational factors and individual differences influence the balance between the two systems. Ayal et al. (2015) reported that individual differences in information processing style are flexible and can be modified by situational factors: instructing participants to adopt an analytical mode of thought improved decision quality, and the benefit depended on how well the induced mode matched the task. Hongdizi et al. (2023) primed analytic processing in two studies (N = 155 and N = 119).
text.formatted: Whether these self-perceptions can vary with immediate context is an open empirical question. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Pacini and Epstein (1999)</ref> noted that both situational factors and individual differences influence the balance between the two systems. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Ayal et al. (2015)</ref> reported that individual differences in information processing style are flexible and can be modified by situational factors: instructing participants to adopt an analytical mode of thought improved decision quality, and the benefit depended on how well the induced mode matched the task. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Hongdizi et al. (2023)</ref> primed analytic processing in two studies (N = 155 and N = 119).

text.text: Priming improved convergent thinking but reduced fluency and flexibility on a divergent thinking task, and the effect on divergent thinking was significant only for participants high in rational thinking style, so thinking style moderated the priming effect.
These studies used explicit instructions or primes and measured task performance.
They did not examine entertainment media or selfreported thinking style as the outcome.
Action films combine suspense, time pressure, and emotionally intense scenes with protagonists who often act on instinct and also plan and solve problems under pressure.
Such content could make intuitive, affect-linked responding feel more relevant, and it could also model effortful thinking.

We therefore compared an action-film clip with a nature documentary, an active comparison condition with a similar amount of audiovisual exposure but no character-driven narrative, on the four REI-40 subscales measured immediately before and after viewing.
The study was exploratory, and the hypotheses were non-directional and not preregistered.
• H1: Exposure to the action-film clip would be associated with different changes in rational and experiential thinking scores than exposure to the documentary.
• H2: Rational thinking scores (ability and engagement) would differ between conditions after viewing.
• H3: Experiential thinking scores (ability and engagement) would differ between conditions after viewing.
The study used a two-group pre-test/post-test experimental design with random assignment.
Group (action film or documentary) was the between-subjects factor, and Time (pre-test or post-test) was the within-subjects factor.
The four dependent variables were the REI-40 subscale scores.
The primary question was whether scores changed differently over time in the two conditions.
Sixteen students at a public university in Pakistan took part, eight per condition, with the same gender composition in both (six women and two men).
Fifteen were undergraduate students and one was a graduate student (action-film group).
Age was not recorded.
Participants were eligible if they were university students, understood English (the questionnaire and stimuli were in English), and gave informed consent.
No power analysis was conducted; the sample size reflected course constraints.
With eight participants per group, a two-tailed independent-samples t test at α = .05 has 80% power only for very large standardized differences (about d = 1.5; Cohen, 1988).
text.formatted: With eight participants per group, a two-tailed independent-samples t test at α = .05 has 80% power only for very large standardized differences (about d = 1.5; <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Cohen, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: Block randomization was used to keep group sizes equal.
Four blocks of four placements (AABB, ABAB, BABA, BBAA) yielded 16 allocations, eight to each condition.
The action-film condition was a 40-minute clip from an action film featuring a central fictional character.
The comparison condition was a 40-minute nature documentary, chosen to contain no human character narrative, moral dilemmas, or emotionally engaging social content.
Both were presented in English.

The conditions differ in genre, pacing, suspense, music, arousal, and narrative structure as well as in the presence of a character, so the design compares two kinds of viewing experience and cannot isolate the effect of a character alone.

The Rational-Experiential Inventory-40 (REI-40; Epstein et al., 1996; Pacini & Epstein, 1999) comprises 40 items in four 10-item subscales: rational ability, rational engagement, experiential ability, and experiential engagement.
text.formatted: The Rational-Experiential Inventory-40 (REI-40; <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Epstein et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Pacini & Epstein, 1999)</ref> comprises 40 items in four 10-item subscales: rational ability, rational engagement, experiential ability, and experiential engagement.

text.text: Items were rated on a five-point frequency scale (1 = never,2 = rarely,3 = occasionally,4 = often,5 = very often), which differs from the agreement format commonly used with the REI.

Negatively worded items were reverse-scored (6 minus the response): rational ability items 1-5, rational engagement items 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9, experiential ability items 1, 6, 8, and 10, and experiential engagement items 4, 6, and 9.
Subscale scores are sums of the 10 items (range 10-50), with higher scores indicating stronger endorsement of that thinking style.
At post-test, participants were asked to respond according to how they were thinking and feeling at that moment.
Internal consistency is reported in the Results.
Participants gave written informed consent and received a general description of the study without the specific hypotheses, to limit demand characteristics.
They completed the REI-40 as a baseline, watched the clip assigned to their condition, and completed the REI-40 again immediately afterwards.
Participants were then debriefed, the reason for withholding the hypotheses was explained, and they were reminded that participation was voluntary and that they could withdraw their data.
All subscale scores were computed from the item-level responses, not from pre-computed summary columns.

Three item responses (0.2% of all item responses; all in the documentary group) were missing and were replaced with the participant's mean on the answered items of the same subscale, so that sum scores stayed on the 10-50 scale.

One participant's gender differed between their pre-test and posttest rows (documentary group), and one post-test row carried an invalid education code (action-film group); demographic information was therefore taken from the pre-test rows.
Change scores were calculated as post-test minus pre-test, so positive values indicate an increase after viewing.
Analyses were run in Python using SciPy (Virtanen et al., 2020), pingouin (Vallat, 2018), and statsmodels (Seabold & Perktold, 2010).
text.formatted: Analyses were run in Python using SciPy <ref type="bibr">(Virtanen et al., 2020)</ref>, pingouin <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Vallat, 2018)</ref>, and statsmodels <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Seabold & Perktold, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The primary analysis was a 2 (Group) × 2 (Time) mixed-design ANOVA for each subscale, with the Group × Time interaction as the test of whether the groups changed differently (sphericity is not an issue with two time levels).

Supporting analyses were independentsamples t tests for baseline and post-test group differences, paired-samples t tests for change within each group, an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) of post-test scores with the pre-test score as covariate (Vickers & Altman, 2001), and nonparametric checks (Mann-Whitney U and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests).
text.formatted: Supporting analyses were independentsamples t tests for baseline and post-test group differences, paired-samples t tests for change within each group, an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) of post-test scores with the pre-test score as covariate <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Vickers & Altman, 2001)</ref>, and nonparametric checks (Mann-Whitney U and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests).

text.text: Effect sizes were Cohen's d for independent comparisons, dz for paired comparisons, and partial eta squared (η²p) for ANOVA effects (Lakens, 2013).
text.formatted: Effect sizes were Cohen's d for independent comparisons, dz for paired comparisons, and partial eta squared (η²p) for ANOVA effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Lakens, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Because four outcomes were analyzed, Holmadjusted p values (Holm, 1979) are reported for the interaction tests, and a Bonferroni threshold of α = .0125 was used to read the within-group tests.
text.formatted: Because four outcomes were analyzed, Holmadjusted p values <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Holm, 1979)</ref> are reported for the interaction tests, and a Bonferroni threshold of α = .0125 was used to read the within-group tests.

text.text: Reliability was estimated with Cronbach's (1951) alpha.
text.formatted: Reliability was estimated with <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Cronbach's (1951)</ref> alpha.

text.text: All tests were two-tailed.
The study was exploratory and small, so results are reported with 95% confidence intervals and should be read as estimates, not as confirmations.
The action-film clip produced no reliable change in self-reported thinking styles relative to the documentary.
Sixteen participants completed the REI-40 before and after viewing (documentary group n = 8; action-film group n = 8), and there were no missing participants.
The sample comprised 12 women and 4 men, with 6 women and 2 men in each group.
Reliability.
Internal consistency (Cronbach's α) was computed for each subscale on the combined sample (N = 16) separately at pre-test and post-test (Table 1).
text.formatted: Internal consistency (Cronbach's α) was computed for each subscale on the combined sample (N = 16) separately at pre-test and post-test (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Reliability was adequate (α ≥ .70) only for rational ability and experiential engagement at post-test, and marginal for rational engagement (α = .65-.68) at both time points.
Experiential ability was unreliable (α = .44 at pre-test and -.24 at post-test).
Estimates based on 16 cases are themselves unstable, but the experiential ability results should be interpreted with particular caution.
Assumptions.
The paired differences and ANCOVA residuals did not depart significantly from normality (Shapiro-Wilk p > .15 in every case; with n = 8 this test has little power).
text.formatted: The paired differences and ANCOVA residuals did not depart significantly from normality (Shapiro-Wilk p > .15 in every case; with n = 8 this test has little power).

text.text: Variances were similar across groups except for rational ability, where Levene's test was significant at pre-test (p = .033) and post-test (p = .018) because the documentary group's scores were more variable.
Welch tests and Mann-Whitney tests for that subscale gave the same conclusions as the standard tests.
Table 2 shows the means and standard deviations at both time points.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> shows the means and standard deviations at both time points.

text.text: At baseline, the two groups did not differ significantly on any subscale (Table 3).
text.formatted: At baseline, the two groups did not differ significantly on any subscale (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>).

text.text: The action-film group had a lower baseline rational engagement score than the documentary group (27.50 vs.
32.62), a large difference that fell just short of significance, t(14) = -2.08, p = .056, d = -1.04, 95% CI of the difference [-10.41, 0.16].

Because chance baseline differences of this size are possible with such small groups, post-test comparisons were supplemented with analyses that account for pre-test scores (see the mixed ANOVA and ANCOVA below).
After viewing, the groups did not differ significantly on any subscale (Table 3).
text.formatted: After viewing, the groups did not differ significantly on any subscale (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>).

text.text: The largest posttest difference was in rational engagement, where the action-film group scored lower than the documentary group, t(14) = -1.73, p = .106, d = -0.86, which largely reflects the baseline difference reported above.
Rational ability, t(14) = -0.93, p = .368, d = -0.47; experiential ability, t(14) = 0.26, p = .801, d = 0.13; and experiential engagement, t(14) = 0.57, p = .580, d = 0.28, did not differ.
Mann-Whitney tests agreed (all p ≥ .187).
The post-test scores therefore provide no evidence that the action-film group scored higher than the documentary group on any subscale.
Documentary group.

Experiential ability decreased from pre-test to post-test (33.88 to 31.00), a mean change of -2.88, 95% CI [-4.99, -0.76], t(7) = -3.21, p = .015, dz = -1.14; the Wilcoxon test was also significant (p = .031).
This p value is below .05 but above the Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of .0125.
Rational ability, rational engagement, and experiential engagement did not change significantly (all p ≥ .396; Table 4).
text.formatted: Rational ability, rational engagement, and experiential engagement did not change significantly (all p ≥ .396; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>).

text.text: Action-film group.
None of the four subscales changed significantly from pre-test to post-test (all p ≥ .431; Table 4).
text.formatted: None of the four subscales changed significantly from pre-test to post-test (all p ≥ .431; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>).

text.text: The mean changes were small relative to their variability: rational ability -1.25, rational engagement +0.62, experiential ability -0.12, and experiential engagement -0.88.
The confidence intervals are wide and include both small decreases and moderate increases (for example, rational engagement [-1.78, 3.03]).
Table 5 presents the mixed ANOVA results.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">5</ref> presents the mixed ANOVA results.

text.text: The Group × Time interaction was not significant for rational ability, F(1, 14) = 1.32, p = .270, η²p = .09; rational engagement, F(1, 14) = 0.35, p = .565, η²p = .02; or experiential engagement, F(1, 14) = 0.07, p = .795, η²p = .01.
The interaction was significant for experiential ability, F(1, 14) = 4.94, p = .043, η²p = .26.
This interaction does not survive correction for four outcomes (Holm-adjusted p = .173), and the Mann-Whitney comparison of change scores was borderline (U = 51, p = .050).
It is also not driven by an increase in the action-film group.

The documentary group's experiential ability fell by 2.88 points, whereas the action-film group's scores stayed essentially unchanged (-0.12); the difference in change between groups was 2.75 points, t(14) = 2.22, p = .043, d = 1.11.
Given the poor reliability of this subscale (Table 1), this result is best treated as tentative.
text.formatted: Given the poor reliability of this subscale (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>), this result is best treated as tentative.

text.text: The main effect of Time was significant only for experiential ability, F(1, 14) = 5.88, p = .029, η²p = .30, which reflects the documentary group's decline.
No main effect of Group was significant (all p ≥ .068); the closest was rational engagement, F(1, 14) = 3.90, p = .068, η²p = .22, consistent with the lower baseline in the action-film group.

Because the groups differed (non-significantly) at baseline on rational engagement, post-test scores were also compared with an ANCOVA that adjusted for pre-test scores (Table 6).
text.formatted: Because the groups differed (non-significantly) at baseline on rational engagement, post-test scores were also compared with an ANCOVA that adjusted for pre-test scores (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_4">6</ref>).

text.text: Pre-test scores strongly predicted post-test scores for every subscale (pre-post correlations from .60 to .88).

After adjustment, the groups did not differ significantly on rational ability, F(1, 13) = 1.11, p = .311, η²p = .08; rational engagement, F(1, 13) = 0.01, p = .936, η²p = .00; experiential ability, F(1, 13) = 3.02, p = .106, η²p = .19; or experiential engagement, F(1, 13) = 0.19, p = .671, η²p = .01.

The homogeneity-of-slopes assumption held for rational engagement, experiential ability, and experiential engagement (all p ≥ .516) but not for rational ability (p = .023), so the rational ability ANCOVA should be read cautiously; the mixed ANOVA and t tests for that subscale agree with it.
H1 (the action-film clip would be associated with different changes in rational and experiential thinking scores than the comparison condition) was not supported.
Group × Time interactions were nonsignificant for rational ability, rational engagement, and experiential engagement.

The single nominally significant interaction, for experiential ability, did not survive correction for multiple outcomes, concerned an unreliable subscale, and reflected a decrease in the documentary group rather than an increase in the action-film group.
H2 (rational thinking scores would differ between conditions after viewing) was not supported.
Neither rational ability nor rational engagement differed between the groups at post-test, in the mixed ANOVA, or after adjusting for pre-test scores.
H3 (experiential thinking scores would differ between conditions after viewing) was not supported.
Experiential ability and experiential engagement did not differ between the groups at post-test or after adjustment.
Overall, the data do not show that viewing an action-film clip changed self-reported rational or experiential thinking styles relative to viewing a nature documentary.

The only nominally significant effects (a decline in experiential ability in the documentary group and the associated interaction) are small-sample findings on a subscale with unacceptable reliability and should be treated as exploratory.
With eight participants per group, the study could detect only very large effects, so the absence of significant differences does not rule out small or moderate effects.
This pilot experiment asked whether watching a 40-minute action-film clip changes self-reported rational and experiential thinking styles relative to watching a nature documentary.
It found no evidence that it does.
The Group × Time interaction was not significant for rational ability, rational engagement, or experiential engagement.
The groups did not differ at post-test on any subscale, and adjusting for pre-test scores did not change that conclusion.
None of the three hypotheses was supported.
The one nominally significant interaction, for experiential ability, should be read with caution for four reasons.
First, it did not survive correction for four outcomes (Holm-adjusted p = .173).
Second, it arose because experiential ability fell in the documentary group (33.88 to 31.00), not because it rose after the film (31.50 to 31.38).
Third, this subscale was unreliable in the present data (α = .44 at pre-test and -.24 at post-test), so differences in its sum scores may largely reflect noise.
Fourth, the comparison condition was not psychologically neutral.
A decline after a long, low-arousal documentary could reflect calm, boredom, fatigue, or the effect of completing the same inventory twice in one session, and the design cannot tell these apart.
The result is a hypothesis for future work, not a finding about nature footage or action films.
Previous studies show that situational manipulations can shift processing mode when they target it directly.

Instructing people to think analytically improved decision quality (Ayal et al., 2015), and priming analytic processing changed performance on convergent and divergent thinking tasks, with thinking style moderating the divergent effect (Hongdizi et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Instructing people to think analytically improved decision quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ayal et al., 2015)</ref>, and priming analytic processing changed performance on convergent and divergent thinking tasks, with thinking style moderating the divergent effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Hongdizi et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Those manipulations were explicit and their outcomes were task performance.

The present manipulation was an entertainment clip, and the outcome was self-described thinking style, which the REI was designed to capture as an individual difference (Epstein et al., 1996; Pacini & Epstein, 1999).
text.formatted: The present manipulation was an entertainment clip, and the outcome was self-described thinking style, which the REI was designed to capture as an individual difference <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Epstein et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Pacini & Epstein, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: A null result here is therefore compatible with the view that such self-ratings are relatively insensitive to brief, indirect exposure, although a study with this sample size cannot establish that.
Theories of identification and narrative transportation (Cohen, 2001; Green & Brock, 2000; van Laer et al., 2014) concern absorption in a story and story-consistent beliefs.
text.formatted: Theories of identification and narrative transportation <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Cohen, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Green & Brock, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">van Laer et al., 2014)</ref> concern absorption in a story and story-consistent beliefs.

text.text: We measured neither, so we cannot say whether participants identified with the film's protagonist or were transported by the story, and the null result does not speak to those processes.
The sample was very small (N = 16), made up of university students and mostly women, so effect estimates are imprecise and generalization is limited.

Small samples have low power and tend to give unstable and inflated effect estimates (Button et al., 2013), which is why confidence intervals are reported throughout and why the absence of significant effects does not rule out small or moderate ones.

text.text: The two groups differed, at a level just short of significance, in baseline rational engagement (d = -1.04).
The stimuli differed in many respects besides the presence of a character, including genre, pacing, music, and arousal, so effects could not be attributed to a character itself.
Session-level factors such as time of day and group atmosphere were not examined and may be confounded with condition.
No manipulation check measured identification, transportation, arousal, or mood.
The REI-40 is a self-report measure of perceived abilities and preferences designed to assess relatively stable dispositions.

Administering it twice within one session, with momentary instructions and a frequency response format rather than the agreement format commonly used, departs from standard use and invites practice and demand effects.
Internal consistency was low for experiential ability at both time points and for rational ability and experiential engagement at pre-test, and estimates from 16 cases are themselves unstable.
The study was not preregistered, only immediate effects were assessed, and no behavioral measure of reasoning was included.
Future studies should use larger samples chosen by a power analysis, individually randomized participants, and preregistered analyses.
Stimuli should be closely matched and should manipulate character traits directly, for example analytic, intuitive, and mixed protagonists.

Manipulation checks for identification, transportation, mood, arousal, and character liking are needed, along with behavioral measures of reasoning such as the Cognitive Reflection Test or heuristic-bias tasks, randomized item order at each testing, the standard REI response format, and a delayed follow-up.
Moderators such as need for cognition and transportability are also worth testing.
In this exploratory pilot experiment, a 40-minute action-film clip did not change self-reported rational or experiential thinking styles differently from a 40-minute nature documentary.

The only nominally significant interaction, for experiential ability, did not survive correction for multiple outcomes, involved a decline in the documentary group rather than an increase after the film, and concerned a subscale with poor reliability.
Given the very small sample, the confounded stimuli, and the self-report outcome, the study cannot rule out small or moderate effects.

It does show that large effects of this kind are unlikely to appear on the REI-40 after a single brief exposure, and it offers effect-size estimates and design lessons for larger, better-matched studies.
